title: Little Women
notes: Adapted by Erin Riley. Act One.

lines.text: (At her writing desk, directly addressing the audience.)

Memory is such a powerful thing, don’t you think? It paints pictures of our happiest moments and allows us to take journeys into the past. Our memories call to mind the ones who have left their marks on our very souls. For me, those people are my family, The March family. And those three marvelous girls?
(She indicates her sisters who have been bustling around behind her)

Those are my sisters. Four parts who make a whole. That Christmas lives in our memories as one of the darkest of our childhood. The country was torn apart by a Civil war that had taken our father far from home.
(JO steps back out of the scene and allows the focus to shift to her sisters.
Meg is arranging some fresh pine on the mantel. BETH is at the piano playing carols,
Amy is walking around balancing a book on her head with a clothespin on her nose)
(taking the book off her head & pouting) Christmas won’t be Christmas without presents. It isn’t fair that some girls have plenty of nice things and other girls nothing at all.
We’ve got father and mother and each other.
We don’t have Papa, though. He’s so far away and we don’t even know how long he’ll be gone or if…
(She doesn’t finish the sentence “he’ll come home.”
BETH goes back to her piano and softly begins playing “Silent Night.”)

Now, now. We must think about how much spiritual comfort Papa gives to those suffering. It’s going to be a hard winter and if we can make small sacrifices, we should. (She pauses) Although. I do wish I felt happier about it.
(Indicating MEG) That lovely young lady is Margaret, but we call her Meg. She is the oldest and most practical of we four.
Being poor wouldn’t be so bad if I didn’t have to go to school with odorous girls who laugh at your dresses and label you if your father isn’t rich.
Not odorous, dearest. Odious.
That’s what I said!
(Indicating Amy) That’s Amy. The silliest goose of a baby sister one could ever have, but with the heart of an artist!
I’m glad we’re not a rich family.
Why’s that, dearest?
Didn’t you say that the children you are governess for are always fighting over toys and clothes, even though their Papa is rich?
I did.
We may work hard and do without things we’d like to have, but it seems to me we’re a much happier family because we take care of each other and make our own fun.
(Indicates BETH)
And that’s our shy little Beth - the sweetest and gentlest soul in all the world .
(Others continue miming in the scene. JO addresses the audience.)

Well, I suppose now that you know my sisters, I should make your better acquaintance. I’m Josephine, but the only person who ever calls me that is my great Aunt March. You can call me Jo. Writer, Actor, and Man of the House while Papa is away. (Putting on cloak and bonnet as she crosses to SL) And I’m about to make my grand entrance.
(Stepping into the room.)
WHAT HO, Don Pedro, ye olde scallywag. Show thyself, villain! BETH and AMY
(They run to greet her and help her with her things)
Jo!
You’re home early today!

Aunt March dozed off in the middle of my very spirited reading of Fordyce’s Sermons and I managed to escape! (walking to the fire to warm herself) Jiminy Christmas it’s cold outside. (She starts to whistle a Christmas tune)
Jo! Look at your skirt!
She was sitting too close to the fire, again.
It’s only a little burnt.
(Superiorly) Oh how I detest dishoveled, unlady-like women!
And I detest vain girls who are only worried about reshaping their dear little noses.
(She pulls the clothes pin from AMY’s nose) And it’s disheveled.
That’s what I said!
Stop it, please, both of you. Jo, you’re old enough to turn up your hair and behave better. It didn’t matter so much when we were younger, but you’re a grown lady, now.
I hate that I’ve got to grow up and be “Miss March.” I can’t get over my disappointment at not being born a boy.
Poor Jo. It’s a tragedy, but it cannot be helped. You must try to be content with having a boy’s name and playing brother to us girls.
Or playing the boy roles in your silly drama productions!
And as for your Miss Amy, you are altogether too prim. Putting on airs and mispronouncing words may be amusing now, but if you don’t amend you’ll grow up to be just like Aunt March!
(AMY looks aghast. ALL laugh. Peace is restored.)
Speaking of those silly plays of mine! We’d better rehearse for the performance tomorrow night! Amy, let’s do the fainting scene! You’re stiff as a poker in that!
I can’t help it! I’ve never actually seen someone swoon and I refuse to bruise myself tumbling on the floor like you do!
Just give it a try! Beth? Some music please?
(BETH obliges with deeply dramatic music. JO and AMY set themselves up for the scene)
Are you ready, Meg? (MEG nods emphatically) We’ll begin with my entrance!
(She rushes to the other side of the room, picking up something as a weapon—anything will do.
Then, melodramatically) “Oh ho! So, Lady Zara! The hour of my revenge is upon you! Listen and you shall hear my hounds as they hunt your beloved Rodrigo!”
(MEG howls, ridiculously).
(Wooden) “Rodrigo. Save me. Save me.”
No, Amy! Try it like this. Watch.
(JO demonstrates)
“Rodrigo. Save me! Save me!”
(She faints overdramatically. MEG and BETH applaud, AMY rolls her eyes)
See? Now, once more, but with feeling!
(Howls once more at JO’S cue, perhaps more fervently to encourage AMY)
(Even more wooden than before)
“Rodrigo. Save me, save me.”
(She dances across the floor gracefully and faints onto the sofa in a manner nothing like what JO
just demonstrated.)
You’re hopeless. Do your best during the performance, but if Marmee laughs, don’t come crying to me.
I don’t see how you can write and act such splendid things, Jo. You're a regular Shakespeare!
(Moving back to the writing desk to jot notes)

Not quite, but I do think The Witch’s Curse is rather a nice thing, but I’d like to try Macbeth. I always wanted to do the killing scene. “Is that a dagger I see before me?” (she is excessively overdramatic in her fencing with the imaginary dagger, causing her sisters to laugh) MARMEE enters in her outdoor clothes. She stops and smiles at her daughters playing.
I’m glad to find my girls so merry!
Marmee!
(MEG, BETH, and AMY rush to help MARMEE with her bonnet, her cloak, bag, etc.
Jo turns to the audience and speaks.

For as long as I have memory, we’ve always called our dear mother, “Marmee.” She was one of the most admired women in our town. She spent her days caring for those less fortunate and her evenings loving and teaching us. She was the most splendid of mothers.
(JO joins the scene in progress behind her.)
There was so much to do getting food baskets ready to hand out tomorrow that I couldn’t get
home for supper, but I brought home a treat for you. (She takes a letter from her pocket.)
A letter from Papa!
(ALL crowd around her.) Yes, a nice long letter. He is well and thinks he shall get through the
cold season better than we feared. He sends all sorts of loving wishes for Christmas, and an especial message to you girls..
(As she begins to read, MR. MARCH appears behind them in uniform.
HE takes over in his voice.) “Give them all…”

“Give them all my dear love and a kiss. Tell them I think of them by day, pray for them by night, and find my best comfort in their affection at all times. A year seems very long to wait before I see them, but remind them that while we wait we may all work, so that these hard days need not be wasted. I know they will remember all I said to them, that they will be loving children to you, and will do their duties so faithfully that when I come back to them, I may be fonder and prouder than ever of my little women.”
(MR. MARCH exits. MARMEE folds the letter. The girls are sniffling..)
I am a selfish girl. But I’ll truly try to be better, so he mayn’t be disappointed in me, by and by.
I think too much of my looks, and hate to work, but I won’t any more, if I can help it.
I won’t envy girls with nice pianos and I’ll not to be afraid of people.
I’ll try and be what he loves to call me, ‘a little woman,’ and not be rough and wild.
It does my heart good to see you receive your Papa’s words so faithfully. And now… another surprise!
(MARMEE goes to her cloak and takes something out of a pocket, turning back to her daughters

smiling.) Your great Aunt March sent you gifts. (The GIRLS are clearly excited) With strict instructions not to spend it foolishly! She gives each of you a dollar with her best wishes for a Happy Christmas!
Jiminy Christmas!
Oh, my stars! A whole dollar!?
That’s a fortune!
Goodness! The holiday may be merry and bright, after all!
(Marmee handing each their dollar)
I desperately need new drawing pencils.
I have my heart set on a new bonnet.
(Turning to BETH, who is quietly studying her dollar)
What about you, Beth? How will you use your fortune?
I would like to buy some new sheet music.
Meg, should I get drawing pencils or hair ribbons? I haven’t had new ones in a maternity.
I think you mean, eternity, darling.
(Sighing) That’s what I said!
Perhaps you could buy just a few pencils and then you’ll have money left over for ribbons.
Hair ribbons? Whatever for! You should buy a dictionary to improve your atrocious spelling.
Girls, don’t peck at one another.
(Jo retreats to the desk and Hannah enters the room with a letter)
Begging your pardon, Mrs. March, but that little German lad is at the kitchen door. He brought this note from his Ma.
(To the audience) This is Hannah. She’s been with us since Meg was born and we can’t imagine
our family without her.
Oh dear, it looks like Mrs. Hummel’s new baby is coming early.
But Missus, you’ve only just come in from the cold and you haven’t even had your tea!
I’m afraid there’s no time to lose. (Hannah gets Marmee’s cloak & bag)
Who are the Hummels?
Mr. Hummel was in your Papa’s regiment and was killed in August. His poor wife has five
children and is about to welcome her sixth. (finishes putting on her cloak) Thank you, Hannah. I may be gone awhile.
I’ll take care of things here.
Goodnight, my darlings. (Marmee & Hannah exit)
Goodnight, Marmee/Good Luck!/Be Safe!/Stay Warm!
Suddenly, wishing for new sheet music seems very selfish.
(Picking up MARMEE’s slippers)
Marmee won’t be using her slippers tonight.
(Taking the slippers from Jo)
Look how threadbare they are, she really should have a new pair.
I know! I’ll buy her a new pair with my dollar from Aunt March! I’m the man of the house and I promised Papa I would take care of her.
No, no, I’ll do it. I’m the oldest. It’s my responsibility.
I have an idea! Let’s all of us buy something for Marmee and nothing for ourselves!
That’s a wonderful idea and so like you, Beth! What shall we buy?
Jo, if you buy the slippers, I’ll buy Marmee a nice pair of warm gloves!
And I’ll get her some handkerchiefs! Embroidered ones!
I’ll buy Marmee a small bottle of cologne. It won’t cost much, and I’ll have some left to buy some hair ribbons.
Jiminy Christmas, Amy! You and your hair ribbons!
Come now, we must hurry before the shops close!
(They exit. JO immediately reenters and goes to the writing desk.)

We found shopping for Marmee to be far more satisfying than buying for ourselves. Even Amy decided to forego her ribbons in order to buy the largest bottle of cologne they had. When we returned we wrapped them up in a pretty basket and placed it by the fireplace, with no regrets that we wouldn’t be hanging our stockings this year. MEG, AMY & BETH come marching in with the Christmas basket of gifts. Jo joins them.
(ad libbing) Merry Christmas, Marmee! Surprise! (they are crestfallen when Marmee isn’t there)
Hannah, where’s Marmee?
She’s been out all night helping that family.
Hannah! ( sniffing the air) What do I smell?
Muffins?
Of course, muffins, sausage, flapjacks, and cinnamon apples. It’s Christmas!
(clapping her hands in glee) How wonderful!
How ever did you manage it, Hannah?
Jiminy Christmas! Hannah, you’re an angel from heaven. (she gives her a big kiss on the cheek)
Saints alive! Enough of your nonsense! Come on, now, or it’ll get cold..
(MARMEE enters from outside, looking exhausted.)
Happy Christmas, my loves!
(ALL immediately surround her with a chorus of “Merry Christmas,” kissing her cheeks, taking
her cloak and bonnet, and ushering her over to sit down.)
Welcome home, Marmee! We have presents for you!
For me? Gifts? But how—
With all our love and the finest of compliments from Aunt March.
Oh, my darlings! Your dollars! You shouldn’t have, but your selflessness warms my heart.
Open mine first!
Oh no, breakfast first.
Hannah is right. I’ll open them after breakfast, but first I’d like to say a word before we sit down.

Not far away from here lies a poor woman with a little newborn baby. Five children are huddled into one bed to keep from freezing, for they have no fire. They have nothing at all to eat. Their life is such a struggle since Mr. Hummel was killed. My girls, will you give them your breakfast as a Christmas present? It is quiet for a moment for the girls are hungry & the special food smells so good.
(rallies) I’m just glad you came before we began.
May we go and help carry the things to the poor little children?

You’ve proven your kindness once again, my girls. I’m tremendously proud of you. We will all go and share some Christmas cheer. When we come back we will have bread and milk for breakfast, and make it up at dinnertime.

We sang carols all the way to the Hummels. We must have made quite the parade with our steaming kettles and dishes. The looks of joy on the faces of the children brought us to happy tears. Their mother called us angels from heaven and we did feel a bit of the divine. We had loved our neighbor better than ourselves and it filled us with joy. It also brought us a surprise later that day.
Girls, youz never gonna believe your eyes when you go into supper. It’s a feast!

(coming in from SR) Yes, it seems that Old Mr. Lawrence saw us marching off to the Hummels’this morning and was rather touched. He sent me a note asking if he could send a few trifles for you in honor of the holiday. I could not refuse, and so you have a feast tonight to make up for the bread-and-milk breakfast.

Jiminy Christmas, who’d have thought! I bet the Lawrence boy put the idea in his head. I know he did! He’s a capital fellow and I wish we could get acquainted. Tomorrow I’m going to march over there and thank him in person for such a capital gift!
(Lights fade and ALL, except for JO exit. She goes to put on her cloak and hat and leads us into
the next scene at the Laurence Mansion)
The Laurence family lived in a stately stone mansion on the other side of our garden hedge.
The estate plainly betokened every sort of comfort and luxury, from the big coach house and

well-kept grounds to the conservatory. Yet it seemed a lonely, lifeless sort of house; for no children frolicked on the lawn, no motherly face ever smiled at the windows, and few people went in and out except the old gentleman and his grandson. I was determined to befriend the lonely boy. So, as soon as Mr. Laurence’s carriage drove away, I marched over and found myself waiting in their grand foyer (steps onto the thrust)
How do you do? I’m Theodore Lawrence.
I’m very pleased to meet you, Mr. Lawrence. I’m Josephine March.
I’m not Mr. Lawrence, I’m only Laurie.
Laurie Lawrence - what an odd name. I think I’m going to call you Teddy.
And I’m going to call you Jo, and your sisters are Meg, Amy and Beth.
How do you know that?

(a bit embarrassed but wanting to be truthful) Well, you see I often hear you calling to one another, and when I’m alone up here I can’t help looking over at your house. You always seem to be having such good times. I beg your pardon for being so rude, but sometimes you forget to put down the curtain and when the lamps are lighted, it’s like looking at a picture to see the fire, and you all round the table with your mother. Her face looks so sweet, I can’t help watching it. I haven’t got any mother, you know.”

We’ll never draw that curtain any more, and I give you leave to look as much as you like. I just wish that you’d come over and see us. Mother is so splendid she’d do you heaps of good and we could have such jolly times. Do you think your grandpa would let you?
Maybe - if you asked him - unless you are afraid of him. He can be quite intimidating.
I’m not afraid of anything.
You haven’t met him in one of his moods.

I suppose he is a bit formidable -like a frightful old eagle. I think he must have a tremendous will of his own. When I’ve seen him out walking, his mouth is always grim but his eyes are kind. He isn’t as handsome as my grandfather, but I like him.
(he entered unnoticed during Jo’s speech)
(Clearing his throat, making BOTH jump)
Thank you, Ma’am. (gruffly)
(Advancing on JO)
So, you’re not afraid of me, eh?
(a bit unsteady) Not much, sir.
And you don’t think I’m as handsome as your grandfather?
(She can’t lie) Not quite, sir.
And I’ve got a tremendous will, have I?
I only said I thought so.
But you like me, in spite of it?
(confident) Yes, I do, sir.
Mr. Lawrence laughs.
(laughing) So what have you been doing to this boy of mine?
Only trying to be neighborly, sir. Your grandson could use some company.
You think he needs cheering up a bit, do you?
Yes, sir. Young folks would do him good. My sisters and I would be glad to help if we could, for we don’t forget the splendid Christmas present you sent us.
(looking at Laurie with new eyes) First I must check with his tutor. (calling ) Mr. Brooke!
(entering) Yes, Mr. Lawrence?
How is your student doing with his studies?
(a bit uncomfortable for he doesn’t want to embarrass Laurie) Well, sir, it is the holiday season and that does make it much easier to be distracted..
I suppose it’s to be expected. But do you think your student would suffer from any major setbacks of discipline were I to arrange a social gathering here at the house? BROOKE
(Grinning broadly)
Not at all, sir. In fact, I think it would do him good.
Then it’s decided. We shall have a dance to bring in the new year. I assume dancing is still in fashion? BROOKE Yes, SIR!
(Whoops with excitement) Thank you, grandfather!
(to Jo) You must come with your sisters, unless they think I’m too formidable.
Oh no, sir! How could they when you were so kind to us yesterday! Well, Beth might struggle but she is afraid of everyone.
Well, tell her I won’t take no for an answer!.
(As he’s exiting, clearly amused)
Frightful old eagle, indeed.
(JO, LAURIE, and BROOKE laugh)
Jo March, I do believe you’re a miracle worker!
(LAURIE and BROOKE exit, JO takes off her cloak and hat) .
Mr. Laurence was as good as his word and a beautiful gilt-papered invitation arrived at our door

the next day. There had not been many such occasions since the war broke out and the soiree became the talk of the town! For our part, the whole house was flipped upside down in anticipation of such a grand event. JO steps onto thrust where she is joined by Marmee, Hannah, Meg, Amy, Beth enter from floor to thrust. There is a screen that Jo steps behind & Hannah helps her into her dress.
Mees Jo, where have you been? Come here and we’ll get you dressed right quick.
Oh, how I wish I had new hair ribbons!
No fussing now, dearest. Those ribbons compliment your dress just beautifully.
(Miserable) Marmee, do I really have to go to the party?
I’m afraid you must, for Mr. Laurence has invited you and it would be terribly rude not to go with your sisters.
Beth, dearest, you really needn’t worry! The music alone will be very grand. I heard Sally Moffatt say there will be sixteen musicians!
(Starstruck) Sixteen musicians! Imagine that!
My dears, do you all have your gloves? ALL EXCEPT JO Yes. Marmee.
Jo? Your gloves?
Mine are spoiled with lemonade, so I will go without.
You must have gloves. Gloves are more important than anything else.
Then I’ll crumple them up in my hands to hide the stains.
We can’t dance without gloves so we’ll each wear one good glove and carry a stained one.
Dance? That’s hardly likely! Especially with this.
(She turns and shows a large, burned patch on her skirt.)
Josephine March, when will you learn not to stand too close to the fire?!
No time to fix it now.
You’ll just have to sit or keep your back to the wall.
Look at my girls - growing into such lovely little women. Now hurry off, It won’t do to be late.
Hannah gives a few last primps to their dresses & the girls each give Marmee a kiss good-bye.
Then they turn & go up to main stage as the main opens. Marmee & Hannah exit SL house door
Music starts & Meg & Amy join in the dance. Beth goes to get punch & Jo finds a place to sit. After the dance Laurie goes looking for Jo. He finds her sitting in the conservatory.
So this is where you’ve been hiding.
Not hiding, I just needed to find a place to sit.
Well you can’t sit all night at a dance. Where is your dance card?
My dance card? Why?
(Bows formally)
Miss March, may I have the pleasure of a dance?
I can’t, for I told Meg I wouldn’t, because….(hesitates)
Because what?
You won’t tell?
Never!

(Turns and shows him the burnt patch on the back of her skirt) I have a bad trick of standing before the fire and so I scorched my dress. Although it’s nicely mended, it shows. Meg told me to keep still, so no one sees it. You may laugh, if you want to: it is funny, I know.

(pondering for a moment & then very gently replying) Never mind that - I’ll tell you how we can manage - there’s a long hall out there (gestures off stage) and we can dance grandly and no one will see us. Please come?
What a capital idea!
They exit SR as Meg walks thru ballroom doors & down to thrust, fanning herself profusely.
(immediately following her) Are you all right, Miss March?

Oh, Mr. Brooke! I’m perfectly well thank you. I just needed a bit of fresh air. It is kind of you to check on me. BROOKE Young Laurence tells me you’re the tutor to the King children. Do you like your work?

I can’t say I do, but I get a good deal of satisfaction out of helping my family, so I won’t complain. I only wish I liked teaching as you do. BROOKE I think you would if you had Laurie for a pupil. I shall be sorry to lose him next year.

Going to college, I suppose? (“Meg’s lips asked that question, but her eyes added, “And what becomes of you?”) BROOKE Yes, it’s high time he went, for he is ready. And as soon as he is off, I shall turn soldier. I am needed.
I am glad of that. I should think every young man would want to go - though it is hard for the mothers and sisters who stay at home.
(rather bitterly) I have neither, and very few friends, to care whether I live or die.
Laurie and his grandfather would care a great deal, and we should all be very sorry to have any
harm happen to you. (with more emotion than “proper”)
(immediately cheered & looking intently at her) Thank you!
(Suddenly shy) I think, perhaps, I’ve cooled off enough to go back inside. BROOKE Ah, yes. May I have the honor of the next dance, then?
I’d be delighted. BROOKE offers her his arm, she takes it, and they return to the ball. They pass Amy & Beth who are leaving the ball and stand in “hall” between conservatory & parlor)
If I can’t go home, please find me a place to hide where no one will come talk to me.
How I wish people didn’t frighten you. You could have such a grand time dancing.
Oh no! I just want to sit and listen to the beautiful music.
Well, I suppose there is no harm in that. How about this parlor? (they enter)
Mr. Lawrence notices the girls have left & he follows them.
Beth! Look at this beautiful piano!
Oh my! (She walks to the instrument and puts her hand out to touch up but quickly withdraws it as if it’s too sacred) It’s magnificent!
(stepping into the room) Ladies, I saw you leave the dance and came to see if you are well.

Oh! Mr. Lawrence (feeling she must quickly explain), my sister is very shy in such a crowd. She was hoping to find a place to sit and listen to the music undisturbed. MR LAWRENCE (noticing that Beth has stepped behind the piano to “hide” but is still observing it with great awe). You must be Beth, the musical one. (Beth nods - too afraid to speak)
(putting on her most proper manners) Yes, sir, and I am Amy. (curtsy) We are most grateful for your kind invitation to this party.
(returning her formality with a bow) I am delighted you could attend. .
We should be going, now.
Not at all, you are welcome to stay here as long as you like. No one will bother you. (he turns to leave and then turns back) Does your sister play the piano?
She does very well on our old piano, even though some of the keys stick.
Laurie’s studies prevent him from playing and the piano suffers for want of use. Do you think
Beth could run over and practice on it now and then, just to keep it in tune? She needn’t see or
speak to anyone for I’m shut in my study down the hall and Laurie is upstairs with Brooke.
As Mr Lawrence talks, Beth has inched her way closer - unable to believe what she is hearing.
What a generous offer!
(Forgetting to be shy for a moment) I’m Beth. I would dearly love to come if you are quite sure nobody will hear me - and be disturbed.
Not a soul, my dear.
How kind you are, sir!

(putting his hand on her shoulder & speaking almost in a whisper) I had a little girl once, with eyes like yours…..God bless you, my dear! (turning to Amy) Now I must return to the party. Good evening. (with nod) AMY & BETH (curtsy) Good evening. When he is gone the 2 girls hug each other - overcome with joy.
As Mr. Lawrence returns to the ball, Mrs. Moffet and Mrs. Gardiner are leaving & stop in the
hall outside the parlor.
Beth, you were amazing! You spoke to Mr. Lawrence! Meg and Jo won’t believe it.
I can’t believe it myself.
I’m going to go find them so you can tell them your wonderful news.
(Amy starts to exit, then pulls back.)
Oh no - here come the gossips Mrs. Moffat and Mrs. Gardiner. They will riddle me with questions so I better wait.
(The GIRLS step away from the doorway but still hear the conversation)
Now that you say it, I see it clear as day! As soon as the Laurence boy was presented to society, those poverty-stricken Marches swept in and took over the place!
I am sure Mrs. March will play her cards well.
Best thing that could happen to the Marches after they tossed their money away trying to set up that progressive school.
Mark my words, the sainted Mrs. March has plans for those girls of hers, and if the Laurence boy isn’t a part of it, I’ll eat my cap!
(Both women laugh and their voices fade away.)
Why, of all the nerve! I can’t believe it! Beth! Did you hear—
(BETH is in tears, clearly distressed by the gossip)
Oh Beth! Don’t cry! None of it is true!
Amy, please, I want to go home! JO and LAURIE return, laughing, but immediately stop when they see Beth distraught
Beth! Whatever is the matter?
Jo, we need to leave right away.
(Comforting BETH) Of course. Laurie, will you please get Meg? (LAURIE exits.) Tell me what happened!
We can’t talk of it here, someone might hear us, and Beth is too upset. I’ll get our coats and we’ll meet you at home.
(AMY and BETH exit as LAURIE. MEG, and BROOKE reenter.)
Jo? What is it?
We must leave. Something has upset Beth tremendously, but they wouldn’t tell me what. Laurie, will you forgive us for going so early?
Don’t give it another thought. I’ll see you home.
Good evening, Mr. Brooke. Thank you for the dance, and Happy New Year!
(She exits in haste, dropping her glove as she goes.)
BROOKE Miss March! (He picks up her dropped glove, but she’s already gone. He smiles and puts it in his pocket. He Exits)
(Reentering to address the audience.)

Once we were able to calm Beth down, Amy told us what the gossiping ladies had said. I was ready to go defend dear Marmee’s honor, but of course Mother wouldn't let me. Once again, she shared her infinite wisdom and told us that gossip was never worth repeating and we should put it out of our heads for we knew what the truth was. And the truth was that Laurie became our best friend and beloved brother in no time at all. He was always doing nice things for us, although one particular thing almost ended in tragedy.
Jo joins Meg on the thrust. They are in their room getting ready to go out. Amy enters
(Entering with AMY, who markedly avoids JO)
Where are you girls going?
Never mind. Little girls shouldn’t ask questions.
(she glowers at Jo and then turn to Meg) Do tell me! I should think you might let me go too; for I haven’t got anything to do, and I am so lonely.
I can’t, dear, because you aren’t invited.
(breaking in) Now, Meg, be quiet. You can’t go, Amy, so don’t be a baby and whine about it.
You are going somewhere with Laurie, I know you are.
Yes, we are. Now do be still, and stop bothering.
I know! You’re going to the theater to see The Seven Castles! And I shall go, for Mother said I might see it, and I’ve got my rag money.
(soothlingly) Just listen to me a minute, and be a good child. Mother doesn’t wish you to go this week, because you are still recovering from your cold. Next week you can go with Beth and Hannah.

(pleading & looking pathetic) I don’t like that half as well as going with you and Laurie. Please let me. I’ve been shut up with this cold so long, and I’m dying for some fun. Do, Meg! I’ll be ever so good.
Suppose we take her. I don’t believe Mother would mind, if we bundle her up well.
If she goes I shan’t! And if I don’t, Laurie won’t like it, and it will be very rude, after he invited only us, to go and drag in Amy.
(Aggravated. She sits & starts to put on her boot) I shall go! Meg says I may, and if I pay for myself, Laurie hasn’t anything to do with it.

(angry & stern) You can’t sit with us, for our seats are reserved, and you mustn’t sit alone; so Laurie will give you his place, and that will spoil our pleasure. You shan’t stir a step, so you may just stay where you are.
(enters on main stage and calls “up” to the girls) Meg! Jo! We need to be leaving.
Meg and Jo go to main stage & then all 3 exit SL.
(As Jo starts walking away) You’ll be sorry for this Jo March, see if you ain’t! (she runs off)
(returns & talks to the audience)
The show was as wonderful as a heart could wish, but Amy’s parting threat kept repeating in my

head. Amy and I both had quick tempers, but our semioccasional explosions were always quickly regretted and forgiven. However, I couldn’t shake the foreboding feeling that this evening was going to be different.
How was the show?
Excellent! My head is full of new plots to add to my book, so I’m off to my desk. (she looks for the manuscript)
Has anyone taken my book? MEG & BETH (looking surprised at the question) No.
Amy says nothing but keeps poking the fire.
Amy, you’ve got it!
No I haven’t.
You know where it is then!
No I don’t.
That’s a fib! (taking her by the shoulders & looking fierce)
It isn’t. I haven’t got it, don’t know where it is now, and don’t care.”
You know something about it, and you’d better tell at once or I’ll make you. (gives her a shake)
Scold as much as you like, you’ll never see your silly old book again.
Why not?
I burned it up!
You wicked, wicked girl! I’ll never forgive you as long as I live! (she runs down to the thrust & everyone exits))

(pacing) Have you ever lost years of work in one instant? It was more than I could bear. Marmee talked to Amy who quickly regretted her action, but her meek apology could not douse the fire of my anger. Even Marmee’s imploring that I not let the sun go down on my anger could not cut through the wall around my heart. I was cross and out of sorts the next day so I asked Laurie to go skating. I hoped that would put me to rights - which it did, but in a terrifying way. (exists SL) 2 skaters come out on the thrust and “skate” during Meg & Amy’s conversation.
Meg is sitting on the couch. Amy enters.
Meg, Jo has gone off to skate with Laurie. She promised I should go next time, for this is the last ice we shall have. But it’s no use to ask. She’ll never forgive me.

Don’t say that. You were very naughty, and it is hard to forgive the loss of her precious book, but I think she might do it now, if you try her at the right minute. Go after them and wait until Jo has got good-natured with Laurie, then take a quiet minute and just kiss her, or do something kind and I’m sure she’ll be friends again, with all her heart.
Do you really think so?
Yes, dear. Now hurry and catch up with them. Main Curtain closes slowly during Meg & Amy’s conversation & snow mound is put SR.
Laurie & Jo enter from SL floor onto thrust & start skating.
We won’t be able to cross the pond today. The ice is too thin. Better to stay here and be safe.
Amy climbs up a snow mound and longingly watches Amy & Laurie skating. Jo notices her but
ignores her - not thinking that she should warn her about the thinner ice on that part of the pond.
Amy sighs, shrugs her shoulders, and decides to skate across. SFX of ice cracking & Amy “falls”
into set piece (and lays down behind set piece with hands toward CS).
Amy! No…please God, no! Skating couple stop and gawk at the drama unfolding without knowing how to help.
(flying past Jo & laying himself out on mainstage to grab Amy’s hands) Grab my hand! Don’t let go! Jo - come pull my feet.
Jo skates to Laurie and pulls his feet. The two other skaters come over to help. They pull Amy
completely out from behind the set piece.
(stands on thrust & helps Amy up while taking off his coat and putting it around Amy) We must get her home. She’s soaked through.
(Laurie gets under one of Amy’s arms, Jo gets under the other & they exit SL floor)

(as they are leaving - looks back over her shoulder at other skaters) Thank you for your help! Skaters mime a shocked conversation as they follow & exit SL floor. BLACK OUT. Tech removes the snow mound. Main curtain opens. Amy is lying on couch.
Marmee and Jo are standing behind couch. Marmee is caressing Amy’s head & Jo is tucking in
her blanket.
Are you sure she’s safe?
Quite safe, dear. She is not hurt, and won’t even take cold, I think, since you were so sensible in covering her and getting her home quickly.
(bitterly condemning her hardness of heart)
Laurie did it all. I, oh, Marmee, if she should die, it would be my fault! It’s my dreadful temper!
I try to cure it. I think I have, and then it breaks out worse than ever. Mother, what shall I do? What shall I do! (she cries bitter tears)

Don’t cry so bitterly, but remember this day and resolve with all your soul that you will never know another like it. Jo dear, we all have our faults and it often takes our lives to conquer them, but never think it is impossible. Watch and pray and never get tired of trying.
Amy starts to stir
I let the sun go down on my anger and wouldn’t forgive you. If it hadn’t been for Laurie, it might have been too late. Oh, Amy, please forgive me!
Amy reaches out her arms & they hug. Marmee then helps Amy up & they exit SR.

Harmony was restored to our home and I threw myself into my writing. I finally completed the first short story I felt good enough to sell. I snuck out to deliver my manuscript to the Spread Eagle newspaper. It took me three tries to muster the courage to go inside, only to be told I’d have to wait a week for an answer. I felt conflicted about leaving my manuscript, but soon learned something that roused a much greater conflict within me.
Jo! What are you doing downtown?
Nothing you need to know about.
You are up to some mischief, Jo. What’s your secret?
I haven’t got any.
You know you have- you can’t hide anything, so up and ‘fess.
Why should I?
Well, if you tell, I’ll share a secret I know.
Is your secret a nice one?
Oh, isn’t it! All about people you know, and such fun! I’ve been aching to tell it a long time. Come now, you begin.
You’ll not say anything about it at home, will you?
Not a word.
(in a whisper) Well, I’ve left one of my stories with a newspaperman, and he’s to give his answer next week.
Hurrah for Miss March, the celebrated American authoress! (throwing up his hat and catching it again)
Hush! It won’t come to anything, I dare say, but I couldn’t rest till I had tried, and I said nothing about it, because I didn’t want anyone else to be disappointed.
It won’t fail. Why, Jo, your stories are works of Shakespeare compared to half the rubbish that is published every day. Won’t it be fun to see it in print, and shan’t we feel proud of our authoress?
Where’s your secret? Play fair, Teddy, or I’ll never believe you again.
I may get into a scrape for telling; but I didn’t promise not to, so I will…..I know where Meg’s missing glove is. JO (disappointed0 Is that all?
It’s quite enough when I tell you where it is.
Tell then.
John Brooke has it.
(surprised and displeased) How do you know?
Saw it.
Where?
Pocket
All this time?
Yes, Isn’t that romantic?
No, it’s horrid.
Don’t you like it?
Of course I don’t. It’s ridiculous. It won’t be allowed. What would Meg say?
You promised not to tell
Well, I won’t for the present. But I’m disgusted, and wish you hadn’t told me.
I thought you’d be pleased.
At the idea of anybody coming to take Meg away? No thank you.
You’ll feel better about it when somebody comes to take you away.
I’d like to see anyone try it!
So should I! (chuckling)
I don’t think secrets agree with me. I feel rumpled up in my mind since you told me that.
Race down this hill with me and you’ll be all right.
I shouldn’t, it’s too boyish (looking around & seeing no one she takes off - exiting)
Not fair! (takes off after her)

I was cross with everyone for the next week - especially Mr. Brooke. Nothing could soothe my ruffled feathers until the next edition of the Eagle Gazette came out, but when it did my spirit soared as it never had before. (exits SL to get newspaper) Meg, Amy & Beth are sitting around the living room doing their sewing. Jo comes in and plops on the couch with the paper and pretends to be reading.
Have you anything interesting there?
Nothing but a story. Won’t amount to much, I guess.
(in a grown-up tone) You’d better read it aloud. That will amuse us and keep you out of mischief.
What’s the name?
The Rival Painters
That sounds well. Read it.
(to the audience) And so I did. I don’t think I have ever read with as much feeling as when I read my first published story to my unknowing family. I was shaking with excitement. And when I finished
I like the part about the splendid picture.
I prefer the lovering part. Viola and Angelo are two of our favorite names. Isn’t that queer?
Who wrote it? JO (sitting up quickly with a flushed face and a mixture of solemnity and excitement, declaring in a loud voice) Your sister!
I knew it! I knew it! (Clapping with glee) O my Jo, I am so proud! (gives her a hug and then skips around singing)
(jumping up and grabbing the paper from Jo) Look at that. Miss Josephine March. (pulls Jo up from couch and spins her around)
(dancing around) Marmee! Hannah! Come quick! Jo’s story is in the paper! Jo’s story is in the paper!
Hannah and Marmee come running in from the kitchen (SR) with hands covered in flour.
Sakes alive, they’ve gone crazy!
(wiping her hands off on her apron) Girls! What is this all about?
(grabs the paper and puts it in front of Marmee’s face) THIS! Jo’s first published story!
(wipes her hands on her apron and then takes the paper with Hannah looking on) “The Rival Painters” by Miss Josephine March. Oh Jo! I can’t believe my eyes!
(starts dancing with the girls) Lordie! Miss Jo - you’re famous!
(beaming) Far from it, but it’s a start.
(putting paper down & hugging Jo) We’re so proud of you, Jo!
This calls for a celebration! Who wants some hot cider and biscuits?
Everyone exits to kitchen SR with Jo going last. She pauses and returns to talk to audience.

I couldn’t imagine ever being happier than I was that day, but I soon learned that happiness for those you love is equally satisfying - especially when the person is the sweetest, gentlest soul in the whole world - my Beth. She had worked for days making embroidered slippers to give to Mr. Lawrence as a thank you for allowing her to practice on his beautiful piano. Laurie had delivered them for her because she was too afraid to do it herself. We expected him to acknowledge her gift, but not in the way he chose.
Oh, Marmee! It’s so grand! Is it for Beth?
Yes, Mr. Lawrence sent it over this afternoon with this note.
It’s so beautiful, Beth will be afraid to touch it!
I am SO happy for Beth!
Here she comes!
(BETH enters, taking off her cloak)
Marmee, Mrs. Hummel wanted to know if you’d be coming to visit—
(BETH notices they’re all standing around the piano, smiling. She walks toward them.)
That can wait, my love. Mr. Lawrence sent you a note, and a gift. (they all step away from the piano)
(She gasps & is too awestruck to speak for a second) For me?
(runs to Beth and hugs her) Yes, all for you, my precious! Isn’t it splendid of him?
What does he write you, Beth?
You read it, Marmee. I can’t. Oh, it is too lovely! (Beth hides her face in Jo’s apron, quite overwhelmed by her present)

(takes out the note & reads) Miss March: Dear Madam, “I have had many pairs of slippers in my time, but I never had any that suited me so well as the ones you’ve fashioned for me. They will always remind me of the gentle giver. I am a man who likes to repay my debts, so I know you will allow “the old gentleman” to send you something which once belonged to the little granddaughter he lost. Your grateful friend and humble servant. James Lawrence.”

(soothing Beth who was still holding onto her by stroking her hair) There, Beth, that’s an honor to be proud of, I’m sure! Laurie told me how fond Mr. Laurence used to be of the child who died, and how he kept all her little things carefully. Just think, he’s given you her piano!

“Your humble servant, James Laurence” - only think of his writing that to you! HANNAH (who came from the kitchen when Amy got home to observe this beautiful moment and has been dabbing her eyes with her apron, says gently) Try it, honey.
Yes, dearest! Sit down, Let’s hear how it sounds!
(BETH sits and begins to play softly on the piano as they stand around and listen.
There is a knock at the door and Hannah goes to answer it.
MR. LAURENCE and LAURIE enter. MARMEE turns and smiles.)
(nodding to Mrs. March) Madam, please pardon the interruption. I only wanted to inquire as to whether Miss Beth received the gift I sent, but I can see she has.
Mr. Laurence! We are so grateful to you for your generosity. Won’t you stay for tea?
Regrettably, we have an engagement in town and cannot stay. I just wanted to ensure the piano was delivered safely. Ladies, we wish you a good day, don’t we Theodore.
Indeed.
(He acknowledges them – all manners)
Mrs. March. Ladies. (beat) Jo.
(MR. LAURENCE and LAURIE turn to leave.)
(Springing up from the piano)
Wait!
What is it, my dear?
I… I…
Not still bashful, are we?
(BETH runs forward and hugs MR. LAURENCE, who, like everyone else, is shocked.)
Thank you!
(MR. LAURENCE returns her hug and they all smile at one another, exiting the stage so only JO
remains. Laurie & Mr. Lawrence SL and the others SR)
Our home was filled with Beth’s beautiful music and our hearts overflowed with gratitude, but as happens in life, the pendulum swung and we found ourselves facing some dark challenges.
There is a knock at the door and Jo goes to answer it. Laurie enters.
I’ve come to see if anyone wants to join me for a drive. I’ve been working away at mathematics till my head is in a muddle, and I’m going to freshen my wits by a brisk turn.
Marmee & Meg have entered SR with sewing baskets and sit to work.
Much obliged, but I’m busy.
I’ll get Amy and Beth. We’ll be ready in a minute. (exits)
(affectionately) Can I do anything for you Madam Mother?

Could you call at the post office? It's our day for a letter but the postman hasn’t been by. Father is as regular as the sun. Another knock/ring brings Hannah to answer the door. She returns frazzled.
Lord help us, it’s one of them horrid telegraph things! Jo, Amy & Beth have just entered with cloaks in hand. Everyone stops & listens breathlessly.
They rush to Marmee’s side, as does Meg. Marmee takes the telegram, reads the 2 lines & falls
back in her chair - white with fear/shock.
(taking the paper from Marmee, reads in a frightened voice) Your husband has been injured. Come at once. S. Hale, Union Hospital, Washington.
I shall go at once, but it may be too late. O children, children; help me to bear it!
The girls all hold onto their mother, quietly sobbing.
The Lord keep the dear man! I won’t waste no time a cryin’, but git your things ready right away,
mum.” (wiping her face on her apron - she exits)
(lifting her head & sitting up straight - pale but steady) Hannah’s right. There’s no time for tears now. Be calm, girls, and let me think.

(having stepped back to try to give the family privacy, now comes forward) Please, ma’am. Let me do something! MARMEE (gathering herself Send a telegram saying I’ll come at once. I’ll take the late train tonight.
What else? The horses are ready. I can go anywhere, do anything.
Please drop Jo at Aunt March’s? I will write a note for you to take to her, Jo. Beth, go and ask
Mr. Laurence for a couple bottles of medicinal wine. I’m not too proud to beg for Father. Amy,
tell Hannah to get down the black trunk, and Meg, come help me find my things.

We all scattered like leaves before a gust of wind, and the quiet happy household was broken up as suddenly as if the paper (maybe telegram instead of paper?) had been an evil spell. I knew the money for traveling expenses had to be borrowed, but I dreaded the reproach of Aunt March, which was sure to come.
Jo steps onto the thrust where Aunt March is sitting imposingly in a chair. JO walks over and
hands her the note from Marmee.
Stand still, Josephine! You’re making me dizzy with your squirming.
(She reads)
I see.
(Folding the note, pointedly.)
Didn’t I say my nephew was a fool to volunteer to go off to war? Of course, I did, but no one listens to me! Oh no!
Please, Aunt March! The telegram said there was no time to waste!
And Forty Dollars! This is an utter fortune! Is your mother planning on throwing a ball in Washington!?
Whatever you can spare would be so helpful, Aunt March, only I must hurry!
You’ll wait until I give you proper leave to go, young lady! Your father had no business running off and leaving his family destitute. And now he goes and gets himself injured!
(angry) We’re enormously proud of Papa, even if you can’t find it in your heart to be kind! It was awfully hard for Marmee to ask you for money, but we’ve nowhere else to turn!
You’re an impudent child! How dare you rush me after having the audacity to ask for a hand out!
I’m sorry I offended you, Aunt March. I know you hate it when people ask for charity.
Josephine! I’ll think the matter over and send an answer by supper and not a moment sooner. In the meantime, I’ll try to forget the lack of manners you’ve displayed today!

I left Aunt March’s fearing my temper may have frozen Aunt March’s already cold heart. I was desperate that Marmee would have the money she needed, so I took matters into my own hands. Some say I was rash, but I would do it again for any one of those I love so dearly. (exits)
Everyone is congregated in living room to see Marmee off, except Jo & Laurie & Hannah
(to Mr. Lawrence) I can’t thank you enough for allowing Mr. Brooke to accompany me.
It is nothing. I have commissions that he can do for me in Washington.
(technically speaking to Marmee, but looking at Meg) It will give me real satisfaction to be of service to you.
(looking at Mr. Brooke shyly but with sincere gratitude) It is such a relief to know that Marmee has someone to take care of her.
(enters) I brought the carriage around & loaded your trunk. We should be going soon.
(enters with basket) I packed supper for you to eat on the train.
Thank you, Hannah.
I can’t imagine what’s keeping Jo. She’s going to miss seeing you off.
(runs in and hands an envelope to Marmee) That’s my contribution toward making Father comfortable and bringing him home.
(looking in the envelope) Twenty five dollars! Jo, I hope you haven’t done anything rash?’
No, it’s mine honestly. I didn’t beg, borrow, or steal it. I earned it! And I don’t think you’ll blame me, for I only sold what was my own.
Your hair!
Oh Jo, how could you?
Your one beauty!
My dear girl, there was no need of this.
She doesn’t look like my Jo any more but I love her dearly for it!
Jiminy Christmas!
I wasn’t sure if Aunt March would lend us the money so I had to do something. When I saw locks of hair for sale in the barber’s window, I went in and asked what he’d give me for my hair.
I fear you’ll have regrets, for Aunt March did send over the money.
No, I won’t regret it. I want Father to have everything he needs to get well. It will do my brains good to have that mop taken off; and it’s good for my vanity. I was getting too proud of my wig.
(hugging Jo) I know your father will be very proud of your sacrifice.
If we’re to make the train, we must be going.
(putting her arms out for a group hug) Come children, give me a hug and promise you’ll be good and do your duties cheerfully.
You don’t worry about nothing but getting Mr. March home.
Everyone exits, except Jo.

I cried myself to sleep that night. I wish I could say that all the tears were for Mother and Father, but I have to admit that a few were for the loss of my one beauty. We were all determined to do as Marmee asked, but when December came around and we were facing a Christmas without our Father and Mother, we started feeling sorry for ourselves. We thought life couldn’t get any harder, but we were about to learn that life itself is a gift to be grateful for, no matter what our circumstances.
Beth is kneeling next to the couch with her head resting on the couch & a bottle of belladono on
the floor next to her and a book open on the couch next to her.
(runs over to Beth) Christopher Columbus! What’s the matter?
(lifts her head and puts up her hand to signal Jo not to come near her) You’ve had the scarlet fever, haven’t you?
Years ago, when Meg did. Why?
Then I’ll tell you. Oh, Jo, the baby’s dead!
What baby?
Mrs. Hummel’s. It died in my lap before she got home!”
How dreadful! I should not have let you go to the Hummels.

It wasn’t dreadful, Jo, only so sad! Mrs. Hummel had gone for a doctor, so I took the baby from his sister so she could rest. It seemed asleep, but all of a sudden it gave a little cry, and trembled, and then lay very still. I tried to warm its feet but it didn’t stir, and I knew it was dead.
Don’t cry, dear! What did you do?

I just sat and held it softly till Mrs. Hummel came with the doctor. He said it was dead and looked at the other children who have sore throats. “Scarlet fever, ma’am. ‘Aught to have called me before”, he said crossly. Then he turned round all of a sudden and told me to go home and take belladonna right away, or I’d have the fever, too.
No you won’t! (hugging Beth close with a frightened look). O Beth, if you should be sick I never could forgive myself! What shall we do!?

Don’t be frightened. I guess I shan’t have it badly. I looked in Mother’s book, and saw that it begins with headache, sore throat, and queer feelings like mine, so I did take some belladonna, and I feel better.
If Mother was only at home! (grabs the book & reads quickly as Meg enters)
Beth! What’s wrong?
It’s scarlet fever. Go get Hannah! (Meg turns around and runs to kitchen) You’ve been over to the baby every day for more than a week, Beth, so I’m afraid you are going to have it.
Hannah and Meg return

Now don’t you all go worrying. Lots of people get scarlet fever and if rightly treated, nobody dies. Let’s get you in bed and have the doctor come take a look. We’ll send Ms. Amy off to Aunt March’s for a spell, to keep her out of harm’s way, and one of you girls can stay at home to amuse Beth while she gets well.
I shall, because it’s my fault she is sick. I told Mother I’d visit the Hummel’s and I haven’t.
Amy will be home soon. I’ll tell her and help her pack.
Hannah & Jo help Beth up and exit SR. Meg wrings her hands & paces.
Amy enters SL with coat and school books or lunch basket)
Amy, Beth caught scarlet fever from the Hummels and Hannah says you need to go stay with Aunt March to keep you safe because you’ve never had it.
I’d rather get Scarlet Fever than live with Aunt March! I won’t go!
You must! Now stay here while I pack your things. When Laurie comes we’ll have him take you. exits
(throwing a tantrum) I won’t go! I won’t. I won’t! (plops down on the couch and starts crying)
(enters SL and sees Amy crying) What’s all this? Did someone upset you at school?
(talking very fast)
Beth caught scarlet fever from the Hummels and I’ve never had it so Hannah says I have to go
live with Aunt March but I don’t want to go. She scares me and I’ll be all alone. I can’t go! I just can’t! (puts her head in her hands and starts crying again)

(sits down beside her) Now be a sensible little woman, and do as they say. Don’t cry, but hear what a jolly plan I’ve got. You go to Aunt March’s, and I’ll come and take you out every day, driving or walking, and we’ll have capital times. You don’t want to be sick- for scarlet fever is no joke, Miss.
(resigned) I don’t know how I’ll bear it, but I’ll try.
Laurie & Amy exit and Jo enters.
(to the audience)
At first the doctor said he thought Beth would have it lightly, but as the days wore on, he looked

more and more sober. Hannah refused to let us tell Marmee because “Mees. March has enough on her plate taking care of your Pappa.” Beth was very patient and bore her pain uncomplainingly, but there came a time when she did not know the faces around her and called imploringly for her mother. We felt guilty writing letters that made no mention of Beth’s illness but we’d been told to mind Hannah, so we did. Then, finally, the doctor said we’d best send for Mother. It was more than I could bear.
Jo walks to the couch and sits with her head in her hands.
(enters SL) Jo, what is it? Is Beth worse? JO (she stands as Laurie crosses to her.
The doctor told us to send for Marmee.
Oh Jo, it’s not as bad as that?

Yes it is. She doesn’t know us and she doesn’t even look like my Beth. There's nobody to help us bear it and God seems so far away I can’t find Him. (Jo clasps her hands together in front of her as if praying and Laurie takes her hands in his).
I’m here. Hold on to me, Jo dear! (Jo bends her head and sobs while Laurie strokes her head as he’d seen her mother do).
(looking up) Thank you, Teddy, I’m better now. (she sits again)
Keep hoping for the best; that will help you, Jo. Soon your mother will be here and then everything will be right.
The telegram was just sent. The soonest she could arrive is late tomorrow. What if she’s too late?
No, she’ll be here late tonight because I telegraphed her yesterday. Are you glad I did?
O Laurie! I am so glad!! How can I ever repay you!?
(with a twinkle in his eye) I’ll send in my bill, by and by - but now I must go fetch your Mother so all can be right. (exits)

It seemed like an eternity before Marmee arrived. The house was still as death, and nothing but the wailing of the wind broke the deep hush. We waited and begged God to spare our sweet sister. Then it happened - she stopped thrashing & lay still. We feared she was dead, but Hannah felt her head and listened at her lips and whispered, “Praise be God, the fever’s turned!” When
Marmee arrived shortly after, Beth was sleeping peacefully and the dreadful pallor was gone. It
was just as Laurie said - all felt right with Marmee home.
(enters SL with Laurie) I am so glad to be home! Aunt March’s house may be luxurious, but our home is worth far more for it is filled with love.
(enters SR) Amy! (Amy runs to give her sister a hug)
Can I see Beth?
Not yet, she’s still very feeble and the doctor said her heart has been weakened. It could take months to restore her health.
With your Mother’s care and her sister’s love, I predict she’ll be downstairs by Christmas.
And Laurie was right again. With a little help Beth was settled on the couch Christmas morning. We spent the morning sharing simple gifts and basking in the warmth of each other’s love.
I’m so full of happiness that if Father was only here, I couldn’t hold one drop more.
His letter only said he’d be with us soon, so we must continue to be patient,
It would be wonderful to start the new year with Father home.
I wouldn’t set your hopes for it. Traveling in the snow and cold may be too much for Father.
Just a year ago we were groaning over the dismal Christmas we expected to have. Do you remember?
So much has happened in a year. We are not the same girls we used to be.
Laurie come prancing in practically doing a jig and announces with a flourish and a bow.
Presenting a special Christmas present for the March family. Mr March wrapped in scarves and blankets hobbles in with the assistance of John Brooke and
Mr. Lawrence. Total chaos ensues. There are squeals of delight and hugging all around. Laurie
immediately went to Beth to help her join in the merriment. Hannah runs out from the kitchen and declares, “Jiminy Christmas! dropping a tray of cookies. They all laugh.
Please, girls, let’s get Beth and Father settled on the couch.
Everyone clears the way & when the 2 are settled, the girls and Marme form a circle around the

couch beaming at the two they had almost lost. Laurie, Mr. Lawrence, & Mr. Brook stand to the one side, enjoying the beautiful tableau. Hannah - after picking up her spilled cookies - stands to the other side looking on and crying.

(feasting his eyes on each the women surrounding him) I fear it has been a hard year for all of you, especially the latter part of it (looking at Amy) but I trust the lessons learned through your trials will serve you well for the rest of your life. I also trust that the friendships that have been forged over this year (looking at the Lawrences and Brook) will continue to blossom and grow for many years. As for myself, I have found the greatest treasure life can hold - the love of all my little women.

Christmas passed and the invalids happily recuperated together.  I longed for a return to our youthful frolicking but I knew I couldn’t stop the changes that come with age. I decided to confide my concerns to Marmee for I needed her wisdom.
Marmee, I want to tell you something.  It is a little thing but it fidgets me.
Is it about Meg?

How quickly you guessed!  Do you remember that Meg left a pair of gloves over at the Laurences and only one was returned? We forgot all about it till Teddy told me that Mr. Brooke keeps it in his waistcoat pocket. Once it fell out and Teddy joked about it, and Mr. Brooke owned that he liked Meg, but didn’t dare say so because he is so poor.  Now isn’t that a dreadful state of things!
Do you think Meg cares for John?
John!?  How can you call him John?!

Jo, don’t be upset.  We fell into it while at the hospital.  He was so devoted to your father and I that we couldn’t help getting fond of him.  He was perfectly open and honorable about Meg, for he told us he loved her, and only wanted our leave to love and work for her…. and the right to make her love him- if he could. He would then earn a comfortable home before marrying her.
How I wish I could marry Meg myself, and keep her in the family!
(smiling at this odd thought) Jo, I don’t want you to say anything to Meg yet.  We need to let her figure out for herself what her feelings are for John.

There’s no hope. She’s got such a soft heart, she’ll melt like butter in the sun if he talks sentimentally to her and that will be the end of our cozy times together.  Oh why weren’t we all boys?  Then there wouldn’t be any bother!
(Meg enters & sits with with her needlepoint as Jo and Marmee exit SR and BROOKE enters SL)
Good afternoon.  I came to see how your father finds himself today.
He is resting in the study. (standing up) Mother will like to see you. Pray sit down, I’ll call her.
Don’t go - are you afraid of me, Margaret?
(blushing for he’d never called her Margaret before) How can I be afraid when you have been so kind to Father?  I only wish I could thank you for it.
(stepping toward her) Shall I tell you how?
(completely inexperienced in love, she uncomfortably speaks) Oh no, please don’t - I’d rather not.
I won’t trouble you. I only want to know if you care for me a little, for I love you dearly, Meg.
(looking down & speaking truthfully) I ….I… I don’t know!
Will you try and find out?  I want to know so much, for I can’t go to work with any heart until I learn whether I am to have my reward in the end..
I’m …too young.
I’ll wait, and in the meantime you could be learning to like me.  Would it be a very hard lesson, dear?
Not if I chose to learn it..
(taking her hands in his and imploring a bit too strongly) Please choose to learn, Meg.  I’d love to teach you.
(pushing him away) I don’t choose!  Please go away and let me be.
(anxiously) Do you really mean that?
Yes, I do.  I don’t want to be worried about such things.
(desperate) Mayn’t I hope you’ll change your mind, by and by?  I’ll wait, and say nothing till you have had more time.  Don’t play with me, Meg.  I didn’t think that of you.
Don’t think of me at all!  I’d rather you wouldn’t.
Aunt March enters & startles the couple. John quickly exits SR and Meg is totally flustered.
Bless me, what’s all this?  (rapping her cane on the floor)
It’s Father’s friend.  I’m so surprised to see you!
That’s evident. (sitting down) But what is Father’s friend saying to make you look like a peony? There’s mischief going on, and I insist upon knowing what it is.  (raps her cane again)
We were merely talking.  Mr. Brooke came to check on Father.
Brooke?  That boy’s tutor, the one who traveled with your mother?  Don’t tell me he’s fallen in love with you! But you would never accept a man of such lowly position.
Hush!  He’s in the study and will hear.
I don’t care if he hears.  I must free my mind at once.  If you mean to marry this Cook, not one penny of my money will ever go to you.  Remember that, and be a sensible girl.
I shall marry whom I please, Aunt March, and you can leave your money to anyone you like!
Highty-tighty! Is that the way you take my advice, miss?  You’ll be sorry for it, by and by, when you’ve tried love in a cottage and found it a failure.
It can’t be any worse than some people find in big houses. AUNT MARCH puts on her glasses to look at the girl, for she did not know her in this new mood.
She desires to make a fresh start, speaking as mildly as she can muster

Now, Meg, my dear, be reasonable and take my advice.  I mean it kindly. I don’t want you to spoil your whole life by making a mistake at the beginning.  You ought to marry well, and help your family.  It’s your duty to make a rich match.
Father and Mother don’t think so.  They like John, though he is poor.
Your parents, my dear, have no more worldly wisdom than two babies.
I’m glad of it!
This Rook is poor, and hasn’t got any rich relations, has he?
No, but he has many warm friends.
You can’t live on friends. Try it and see how cool they’ll grow.  He hasn’t any business, either. Has he?
Not yet. Mr. Laurence is going to help him get a start.

That won’t last long.  James Laurence is a crotchety old fellow, and not to be depended on.  So you intend to marry a man without money, position, or business and go on working harder than you do now, when you might be comfortable all your days by minding me and doing better?  I thought you had more sense, Meg.

I couldn’t do better if I waited half my life!  John is good and wise; he’s got heaps of talent; he’s willing to work, and sure to get on, he’s so energetic and brave.  Everyone likes and respects him, and I’m proud to think he cares for me, though I’m so poor and young and silly.
He knows you have got rich relations, child. I suspect  that’s the secret of his liking.

Aunt March, how dare you say such a thing!  My John wouldn’t marry for money any more than I would.  We are willing to work, and we mean to wait until he’s settled.  I’m not afraid of being poor, for I’ve been happy so far, and I know I shall be with him, because he loves me and I…
(she stops, remembering that she hadn’t yet made up her mind and that John might be listening)

Well, I wash my hands of the whole affair.  I’m disappointed in you, and haven’t spirits to see your father now.  Don’t expect anything from me when you are married; your Mr. Book's friends must take care of you.  I’m done with you forever!
Aunt March storms off SL and BROOKE rushes in from SR and goes to Meg.
I couldn’t help hearing, Meg.  Thank you for defending me, and thank you Aunt March for proving that you do care for me, at least  a little bit.
I didn't know how much till she abused you.
(taking her hands) So I needn’t go away, but may stay and be happy?
(almost in a whisper) Yes, John.
She hides her face on John’s waistcoat and he wraps his arms around her and pulls her close
Jo enters.
(startled to see Meg wrapped in John’s arms) Jiminy Christmas!

John and Meg were married the summer after the war ended and by the next summer Meg was expecting and presented John with a pair of twins. They were the most beautiful babies, and everyone fell immediately in love with them, except Aunt March, who proclaimed the idea of twins to be “excessive.”  As for me, I was growing restless. I had my writing, but the paper only wanted sensational stories which grew less and less satisfying. I was longing for change, but was not prepared for what was to come.
(enters SL) What ho! Who do I spy before me? Not the fabled literary genius, Josephine March?!
Laurie! What a surprise! (She jumps up and hugs him)
You’ll be shocked to hear I did exceptionally well on my exams! John Brooke ought to be very proud of me!
We’re all proud of you, Teddy.
I’m glad,(looking at her intensely) but your esteem is what I most desire.
Oh Teddy, please don’t!

It’s no use Jo. We’ve got to have it out. I’ve loved you ever since I’ve known you. I’ve tried to show it, but you wouldn’t let me; Now I’m going to make you hear and give me an answer for I can’t go on any longer. (A Beat, she’s listening) I’ve worked so hard to please you, I gave up billiards and everything you didn’t like, and waited and never complained for I hoped you’d love me, though I’m not half good enough.

Yes you are. You’re a great deal too good for me, and I’m grateful to you, and so proud and fond of you. I don’t see why I can’t love you as you want me to. I’ve tried, but I can’t change the feeling.
(grabbing her hands and bringing his face near hers) Really, truly, Jo?
Really, truly,  dear. (Laurie drops her hands and turns away)
O Teddy, I’m sorry, so desperately sorry.  I wish you wouldn’t take it so hard! (Trying to speak sense into him) with our quick tempers and strong wills, we’d be miserable if we were to…
Marry? (hopeful) If you loved me, Jo, we shouldn’t be miserable. I’d be a perfect saint, for you could make me anything you like.
No I can’t.  I tried it and failed, and I won’t risk our happiness by such a serious experiment. We’ll be good friends all our lives, but we won’t go and do anything rash.
(angry) I don’t believe you’ve got any heart!
(pained) I wish I hadn’t!

(talking sweetly - bringing all his persuasive powers to bear) Oh Jo, everyone expects it. Grandfather has set his heart on it – your family will like it – and I can’t get on without you. Say you will, and let’s be happy. Please, Jo, don’t disappoint everyone.
(slowly, with firm resolve) I can’t say yes truly (pause)  so I won’t say it at all.  (speaking faster) By and by, you’ll see that I’m right, and thank me for it.
(anger returns) I’ll be hanged if I do! I’ll never love anyone but you!

(pleading) Teddy, be sensible. You’ll get over this after a while, and find some lovely, accomplished girl who will adore you and make a fine mistress for your fine house.  I shouldn’t.  I’m awkward and odd, and you’d be ashamed of me. We’d quarrel – we can’t help it even now! I wouldn’t like elegant society and you would. You’d hate my scribbling, and I can’t get on without it. We would be unhappy, and we would wish we hadn’t done it, and everything would be horrid.
(sarcastic) Anything more?
(matter-of-fact) Nothing more – except that I don’t believe I shall ever marry. I am happy as I am and love my liberty too well to give it up.

(frenzied) I know better! There will come a time when you will care for somebody and you’ll love him tremendously, and live and die for him. I know you will, because that’s your way. (totally distraught) And I’ll  have to stand by and see it!!  (He runs off)
Jo stands looking where Laurie has run off, shaking her head. She sighs and turns to audience.

I hated hurting my boy, but Teddy deserved the truth and so did his Grandfather. So I gathered my courage and went to Mr. Lawrence to tell him the hard story. There were bitter tears when I told him that I couldn’t make myself love Teddy as he wanted me to. I could see Mr. Lawrence was sorely disappointed but he gave me no reproach. Instead, he promised to take Laurie away to Europe for he shared my fear that Teddy would do something rash. They packed and left quickly, leaving me even more unsettled. I wanted to calm my spirit, but more turmoil was on the way.
Mr. & Mrs. March  & Beth entered during above monologue. Marmee knits in rocker. Mr. March
reads on the couch. Amy is playing the  piano.
(enters SL) I hate to bring bad bad news, but your sister’s carriage just stopped out front.
I can’t imagine why she would be paying us a visit during the week.
I thought Amy went to Aunt March’s to read to her today.
Lord have mercy!  Miss Amy must be sick and is too ill to walk home!
Hannah, it is never prudent to let our imaginations run away with us.
Mr. March is right.  It’s far better to wait on the truth, than imagine the worst.
(always thoughtful) I’ll get the door.
And I’ll make some tea with extra sugar.  Maybe that’ll take some of the sour out of her! (exits)
Aunt March enters SL with Amy at her side & Beth behind.
(standing & offering his seat to his sister. She sits & he sits next to her) Welcome, sister!  Come in and have a seat (gestures to his seat on the couch)
Hannah has just gone to draw some tea for us.
Don’t bother, I don’t plan to stay here one moment longer than necessary.
Are you well, Amy?
Oh, Marmee! I think I may be overcome with excitement (beat) that is -  if you and Pappa agree.
Agree to what, my dear?
I’m getting too old to travel abroad alone, so I’d like Amy to be my traveling companion.

(running to Pappa and kneeling before him) Pleeeease, Pappa! What better way to grow as an artist, than to study the work of the great masters? MR MARCH (looking first at Amy’s pleading eyes and then looking over her head to Marmee to determine how her mother feels about it. Marmee gently smiles and gives a nod. Pappa looks back to Amy)  Alright, but you must remember that your first duty is to your aunt, and only then can you pursue your artistic dreams.
Oh, thank you, Pappa! (she throws her arms around his neck and kisses him on the check.  Then she runs to Marmee to kiss and hug her as well.)
(comes flying in  SL with basket of food & hangs cloak while talking loudly)
The market was particularly chaotic today but I fought my way through and conquered every
task on my list!
I see you are still as boisterous and un-refined as ever, Josephine March.
(turns to see Aunt March with a look of total surprise) Aunt March!  (changes her voice to be “proper” and does a small curstay) Good afternoon, Aunt March. I’m sorry I didn’t see you when I came in.
Jo, Aunt March has come to ask if we’ll allow Amy to go abroad and be her traveling companion Jo’s facial reaction is shock & bewilderment
Isn’t it exciting, Jo!
Amy, why don’t you run in and tell Hannah your news.  I’m sure she’ll want to get started right away on fixing you things for the voyage.
Amy exits as Jo recovers herself & decides to confront Aunt March
Aunt March, do you remember saying that you’d take me to Europe someday?
Yes, but that was before you told me that you don’t like favors. You said you’d rather do everything for yourself and be perfectly independent.  Do you remember saying that?
Jo is unable to speak with the realization that her rebellious tongue had cost her dearly.
(rescuing Jo)
Jo has had several stories published in the paper.  She used her wages to send Beth to the shore.
Such a frivolous waste of good money.

(who has been quietly observing but now is emboldened to defend her beloved Jo) It was frivolous to spend money on me. I tried to say no, but Jo insisted that the ocean air would help me regain my health.

(reaching out his arms to invite Beth to come and sit with him) And you have improved, my dear.  (looking at Jo) It was a magnanimous gesture of love. Jo’s spirit is revived with the high praise of her father.
It’s true, I DO want to be independent and earn a living that can help my family.
(leaving her father to go take Jo’s hand) You ARE such a help to me, Jo.  I don’t think I could have parted with you for such a long time.
(to Mr. March) It is shameful that your girls have to work at all.  You should be encouraging them to marry for money - like that Lawrence boy next door.
(fighting back her anger) Aunt March, let me call Hannah to help you to your carriage.  I know you didn’t want to stay long.
Hannah immediately appears because she has been listening at the door.
Yes’m Mrs. March, I’d be happy to help her to the door!
Mr. March stands and helps Aunt March up.  He bows to his sister and Aunt March takes
Hannah’s arm with dignified indignation as they exit SL. As they exit, Mr. March takes Beth by the hand and they exit SR, leaving Jo and Marmee alone on the stage.

(going to sit at Marmee’s feet) Marmee, do you and Pappa mind that I turned Teddy down?   I know what Aunt March said is true. Marrying “that Lawrence boy,” would mean you’d  never have to worry about money again.

(stroking Jo’s hair) Your father and I would never think like that.  We hope our daughters will be admired, loved and respected; to have a happy youth and wisely marry. But not to marry rich men merely because they are rich, or to have splendid houses which are not homes because love is wanting.  Money is a needful and precious thing - and when well used a noble thing - but I never want you to think it is the first or only prize to strive for. I’d rather see you poor men’s wives, if you were happy, beloved, and contented, than queens on thrones without self-respect and peace.

Oh, Marmee, what would I do without you to steady me? I’m so out-of-sorts.  Meg is busy with her family, I’ve lost “my boy” forever, Amy is living my dream, and I am stuck with nothing to write about but imaginary adventures.  How I long to try my wings.

I do think a change of scenery would be good for you. If you are willing to work, I have a proposal. My friend, Mrs. Kirke, runs a boarding house in New York. She wrote me to ask if I knew of a respectable young person to teach her two girls. She's very kind and would make things pleasant for you, if it would suit you.
Suit me?  It’s perfect! I shall see and hear new things, get new ideas, and even if I haven’t much time there, I shall bring home quantities of material for my rubbish.
Then I’ll go and write at once to make the arrangements. (exits SR)
(talking to the audience)
Beth enters and sits on the couch
I was thrilled that I had  a place to fly to, but there was one shadow that darkened my joy - Beth. Although her health was better since her return from the ocean, she was not her old cheerful self.
She often sat alone staring off, and rarely played her piano. I even found her crying.
(running to her and kneeling before her) Oh Beth, what is it?  Is it the old pain, my precious?
No, it’s a new one, but I can bear it.
Tell me all about it, and let me cure it as I did the other.
You can’t, Jo.  There is no cure. (She clings to Jo and cries)
Please tell me what is troubling you.
Not now…. Not yet…. But I promise to tell you, by and by.
I was coming to tell you that I am going to New York to teach Mrs. Kirk’s girls through the school year, but I can’t leave you like this.

Oh Jo, you mustn’t stay on my account.  You have always dreamed of having adventures and this is your chance.  You won’t be gone as long as if you went abroad and you will write often to cheer me out of my silly sadness.
Beth, sweet Beth, I wish I could take you with me.
No, I belong here with Marmee and Father. We’ll miss you, but the sooner you go, the sooner you’ll return.
(They embrace and JO goes to exit, looking back at BETH, who raises her hand in farewell.
JO exits. BETH follows)
When I finally arrived in New York City I was overwhelmed by the size and noise! I felt very grown up, indeed, when I hired a carriage to take me to Mrs. Kirke’s boarding house.
(MRS. KIRKE enters, carrying Jo’s suitcase.)

I hope you will make yourself right at home here. I’m on the drive from morning to night, but a great anxiety will be off my mind if I know the children are safe with you. There are some pleasant people in the house if you feel sociable, and your evenings are always free.
There is a ruckus as Professor Bhaer and the girls burst into the room. He is growling wildly with Kitty on his back and Minnie wrapped around his leg.
Mercy help us! Girls! What have you done to poor Professor Bhaer?
Mrs. Kirke! Forgive me! You have company!
He really is a bear, Mama! I told you so!
Kitty, get down from the professor this instant!
Now it’s my turn!
(Laughing) I’m afraid not, mein kinder. We’ve upset your Mutter and frightened this young lady!
Ah, yes, this is Miss March! She will be staying with us to teach my daughters. Kitty, Minnie, show Miss March that you have some manners and give her a proper welcome.
Kitty and Minnie give a formal greeting, standing straight together; they speak and curtsy.
It’s a pleasure to meet you, Miss March.
Can you tell wonderful stories like Mr. Bhaer?
Can you make up plays for us like Mr. Bhaer?
It looks like I have a high standard to live up to!
Now for my manners. Miss March, this is Professor Bhaer from Germany. Professor Bhaer, this is Miss March, an aspiring author.
(Professor Bhaer makes a formal bow.)
Itz my pleasure to meet you. Please accept my apology for our behavior. Had I known—
No apology needed. I love a good romp and you make an excellent bear!
The young ladies enjoy teasing me about my name. “Professor Bhaer is our bear,” they like to say! And when they say it, I become a bear for them. It’s only right!
(Recognizing a kindred spirit)
I’d say so!
Well, I shall not disturb you further. Miss March, I am honored to make your acquaintance.
Don’t go!
Please stay!
Nein. I need to let Miss March get settled, but perhaps I will see you at dinner?
Yes, I would like that.
Professor Bhaer smiles broadly at Jo, nods to both ladies, makes a dramatic flourishing bow to the girls, and exits.
Alright, young ladies! Lunch is waiting for you in the kitchen! Skedaddle!
The girls exit in a torrent of noise and joy.
The girls clearly adore Mr. Bhaer.

We all do. He is well-educated, kind and thoughtful to everyone, good natured and generous—even though he’s poor as a church mouse. You see, he gives most of his tutoring money to pay for the education of his two orphaned nephews. I’ve never heard him complain but I think he must be lonely. I do hope some good fortune will come his way soon. But now I must show you to your room and get back to my duties.
(She exits, leaving Jo to talk to the audience once again.)

(standing in a pool of light SR) Dearest Marmee, I love my room in the garret.  It is cozy and warm with a nice little table by a sunny window where I can write.
