I intend to write regular letters and will cherish any news you can send about the family. It is hard not to miss home but I am determined to make the most of this time.  I don’t know if I will write any great literary works here, but I am certain I will make a new friend,  for
Mr. Bhaer is a kindred spirit. I’ll write more about him later.

Love, Jo AMY(standing in pool of light SR) My dearest family, Laurie came to visit me at Christmas and ended up staying for a month.  At first it was very pleasant to share his company and have him notice that I have worked hard to polish myself and make the most of my little things.  However, with time I found his demeanor much changed. He has lost all enthusiasm for life and was content to just be lazy and have me pet him with my sisterly attentions.  I finally took it upon myself to try to rouse him with a lecture.  I told him that it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because he didn’t get the girl he wanted.  I told him he could forget his trouble if he set about another task, like attending to his grandfather’s business.  I am not sure if my efforts had the desired effect, but he did go back to spend the rest of the winter with Mr. Lawrence.  He asked me to write and said he’d be back in the spring.  When he comes, I hope I can introduce him to Fred Vaughn because I have a feeling that Fred is going to propose to me. Love to all, Amy
(standing in pool of light SL) Dear Miss March,
Beth wrote to tell me that you went to New York to work as a governess and pursue your literary

dreams.  I hope you will find what your heart needs.  As for myself, I find that I cannot settle my heart or make plans for my life until I know if there is any hope that you will change your mind. Please write and tell me if you will ever allow me to come home to you and be happy. Theadore Lawrence

(standing in pool of light SR) Dear Mr. Lawrence, I do think that New York will help me find what my heart needs, even if it doesn’t fulfill my literary dreams.  I  hope that your travels will help you find someone who can fill your heart, for I cannot.  There is no chance this will ever change, but when you find another, I hope you will open a small corner of your heart for your loving sister Jo. Josephine  March

Dear Amy, I received your most recent letter and was surprised that you have decided to accept Fred Vaughn’s proposal when he returns in the spring.  What disturbs me the most is your reason for this choice. You are convinced that you will serve your family by marrying a rich man. I know this is not what your parents would wish for you and it is certainly not what I wish for you. Marriage should be built on a strong foundation of love and respect.  Money can bring physical comforts but it does not bring comfort to our hearts. My travels have proved this to me.  My time with you did me more good than all the luxuries of Europe. It is the people we love who warm our hearts and steady us through the storms of life.  I beg you to reconsider this choice. With strong affection,  Laurie

Apart from writing letters, I was determined to find a paper that would print my stories. I gathered my courage and left a manuscript at the Weekly Volcano for their review.  My pleasure in hearing they would print it, was quickly followed by dismay because they had edited out all the morals that I had included as ballast for so much romance. I was told that people wanted to be amused, not preached at.  So my choice was sensationalism and income, or morals and poverty.  My natural desire to make life easier for my family won out.  It was a decision I wasn’t proud of, and was gratefully saved from, by a new friend.
Bhear enters with a paper hat on his head that he is unaware of
I have come for your German lesson as promised.
(suppressing laughter) I can see that you’ve had a busy day with your other students.  I don’t want to be a burden.
It is not a burden, it is my payment for your kindness of mending my clothes. (Jo can’t hold it in and starts to laugh) Had you no respect for me, that you laugh in your teacher’s face?

How can I be respectful, sire, when you forget to take your hat off? “The absent minded Professor gravely felt and removed the little cocked hat, looked at it a minute, and then threw back his head and laughed like a merry bass viol.”
Ah, I see him now. It is my students who make me a fool with my cap.  Well it is nothing.
As the Professor unfolds the cap he sees the title “Weekly Volcano” with a scandalous picture

and he speaks with disgust. I wish these papers did not come in the house.  They are not for children to see, nor young people to read. It is not well, and I haf no patience with those who make this harm.  I would rather give children gunpowder to play with than this bad trash.
The stories might not be bad, only silly and if there is a demand for it, I don’t see any harm in
supplying them.  Many respectable people make an honest living out of these sensational stories.
There is a demand for whisky, but I think you and I do not care to sell it.  If the respectable

people knew what harm they did, they would not feel that the living was honest.  They had no right to put poison in the sugarplum and let the small ones eat it.  No , they should think a little and sweep mud in the street before they do this thing.   (he crumples the paper & throws in fire)

(defensive) What is a writer to do when no one will publish noble stories with morals! BHAER (pauses as he realizes Jo must be involved in these stories to be so defensive, so he answers compassionately)  The writer should wait until they can write from their heart what is good and true. Such a story will find an honorable publisher.
(his compassion having cut through her defensiveness, she is left with her genuine struggle) What if such a story never comes?
Wait for it, my friend.  It may take time, but it will surely come.

I burned all my sensational stories that night and decided to “sweep mud in the street” until I could do better.  I corked up my inkstand and spent more time enjoying the company of Professor Bhaer.  I found myself studying his character to discover what was the charm that made him universally liked.  I decided it was his benevolence and goodwill to all people. This discovery made me care for him more deeply than I was ready to acknowledge.  With a little more time, I might have figured it out, but our time was cut short.
Miss March, I have enjoyed our evening conversations so well that I thought I might be bold enough to ask if you’d accompany me to the theater tonight.
I would love that, Professor, but tickets are so expensive.
I have a plan that will not be so, but first I wish to ask for a favor. Could you call me by my given name - Friedrich? (his look implies the question is about more than his name)
(feeling shy) Yes, Friedrich, but then you must call me Jo.
(stepping closer) Ah, Jo.  Such a dear, funny little name.
(running in with Minnie who is holding a telegram) Miss March, we have something for you.
Mother said it was ok to interrupt because it is very important. (hands her the letter)
Jo? You’ve gone pale. What is it?
